programs.title: Cloud & Systems Engineering
programs.description: Build from packets, operating systems, and identity into cloud platforms, automation, observability, Kubernetes, and recovery engineering.
prerequisites: Basic computer literacy; no prior cloud certification required
Comfort using a terminal becomes useful after the foundation modules
outcomes: Trace a request across DNS, networks, transport, TLS, applications, and infrastructure
Administer Linux/Windows and identity concepts using evidence-based troubleshooting
Design cloud and Kubernetes systems around failure, observability, automation, and recovery
Explain tradeoffs among availability, security, cost, performance, and operational complexity
programs.capstone: Design and defend a resilient service architecture, then reproduce at least one failure/recovery scenario with preserved evidence.

programs.title: Advanced Computing
programs.description: Connect computer architecture, operating systems, memory, parallelism, distributed systems, GPU computing, HPC, and quantum computing.
prerequisites: Programming fundamentals
Basic algebra; linear algebra becomes increasingly important
Operating-system and networking fundamentals recommended for distributed/HPC work
outcomes: Reason about compute from processor/memory architecture through distributed execution
Model performance, parallelism, locality, synchronization, and failure
Explain GPU/HPC design tradeoffs and measurement methodology
Separate quantum-computing mathematics, simulation, hardware claims, and experimental evidence
programs.capstone: Choose an advanced-computing workload, identify its computational bottleneck, build a reproducible model, and defend the architecture and measurement plan.

programs.title: Software Engineering
programs.description: Learn programming, data structures, algorithms, APIs, databases, testing, architecture, DevOps, and production software reasoning.
prerequisites: No framework knowledge required
Basic programming concepts are recommended before advanced architecture modules
outcomes: Translate requirements into testable software behavior
Choose data structures and algorithms from constraints rather than habit
Design APIs, data models, tests, and failure handling as explicit contracts
Ship software through version control, CI/CD, observability, and reversible change
programs.capstone: Build a small service with a documented contract, persistent data, automated tests, failure handling, and a reproducible delivery path.

programs.title: Cybersecurity
programs.description: Learn security foundations, identity, risk, network and application security, endpoint defense, detection, governance, recovery, and secure architecture.
prerequisites: Networking and operating-system fundamentals are strongly recommended
All practical exercises must use owned, isolated, synthetic, or explicitly authorized systems
outcomes: Model assets, trust boundaries, threats, controls, and residual risk
Evaluate identity, network, endpoint, application, and cloud security controls
Reproduce vulnerabilities safely and connect findings to remediation and detection
Communicate security evidence using repeatable methods and explicit authorization boundaries
programs.capstone: Complete an authorized security assessment of a synthetic environment: threat model, reproduce a bounded weakness, remediate it, and verify the control.

programs.title: Technical Leadership & IT Management
programs.description: Develop operational leadership across incidents, ITSM, teams, strategy, projects, vendors, governance, risk, finance, capacity, reliability, and recovery.
prerequisites: Some workplace or project experience is helpful but not required
outcomes: Translate technical conditions into operational and business decisions
Run incidents, projects, services, vendors, and teams with explicit ownership and evidence
Reason about reliability, capacity, cost, risk, and governance together
Communicate decisions, assumptions, uncertainty, and follow-through clearly
programs.capstone: Lead a simulated service review from incident evidence through risk, budget, ownership, reliability work, and an executive decision memo.

programs.title: Mathematics for Engineering & Computing
programs.description: Build algebraic fluency into functions, discrete math, sequences, trigonometry, calculus, linear algebra, probability, and numerical methods.
prerequisites: Arithmetic and basic algebra are enough to begin
Calculus and linear algebra paths provide their own prerequisite bridges
outcomes: Represent technical problems with equations, functions, vectors, matrices, graphs, and probability
Derive results instead of relying only on memorized formulas
Check calculations numerically and interpret assumptions and error
Connect mathematics to software, physics, AI, networks, and advanced computing
programs.capstone: Model a real engineering question mathematically, derive an expected result, compute it independently, and explain the limits of the model.

programs.title: Physics for Engineers
programs.description: Develop mechanics, momentum, rotation, energy, waves, thermodynamics, electricity, magnetism, modern physics, and quantum foundations through models and experiments.
prerequisites: Algebra required; trigonometry and calculus become useful as the course deepens
outcomes: Translate physical situations into models with units, assumptions, and conservation laws
Solve and verify mechanics, energy, wave, electricity, magnetism, and thermodynamic problems
Distinguish idealized models from experimental systems and measurement uncertainty
Connect modern/quantum physics to engineering and computing without overstating what a model proves
programs.capstone: Design a bounded physics investigation with prediction, model, measurement or simulation, uncertainty discussion, and evidence-backed conclusion.

aiResearchPath.title: AI and Machine Learning: Evidence-First Research Path
aiResearchPath.statement: Original independent self-study pathway connecting verifiable open courses and books to reproducible, falsifiable engineering exercises. External resources remain owned and hosted by their institutions; this portfolio does not claim affiliation, credit or certification.
aiResearchPath.assessment: Learners self-record completion in their own browser; a checkbox is not external grading, academic credit, or verified mastery.

stages.title: 01 / Python, experiments and reproducibility
prerequisites: No programming background is assumed
stages.question: How can another learner prove that your code produces the stated result?

checkpoint.prompt: A seeded Bernoulli experiment records 37 successes in 100 independent trials. What is the maximum-likelihood estimate of the success probability?
checkpoint.hint: Divide observed successes by the number of valid trials.
derivation: For a Bernoulli model, the observed log-likelihood is 37 log(p) + 63 log(1-p).
Setting the derivative to zero gives 37/p = 63/(1-p), so 100p = 37.
The sample estimate is p-hat = 37/100 = 0.37; it does not establish the true probability with certainty.
checkpoint.misconception: A fixed seed makes an experiment reproducible, not unbiased or representative.
checkpoint.extension: Repeat at larger sample sizes over multiple independent seeds and report dispersion, not just one estimate.

stages.practice: Implement a seeded Python experiment that estimates a Bernoulli probability from 100, 1,000 and 10,000 trials; write unit tests for invalid inputs and replay the same result with an identical seed.
stages.deliverable: Source, instructions, deterministic tests, and a concise uncertainty interpretation.
acceptance: A fresh run succeeds from documented installation steps
Repeated seeded runs produce identical counts
Input validation fails predictably on invalid samples
Convergence is discussed without claiming every individual run improves

stages.title: 02 / Linear algebra, numerical stability and geometry
prerequisites: Python functions, vectors, algebra
stages.question: When does a numerical solution look plausible but become unreliable?

checkpoint.prompt: For a two-by-two matrix A = [[1, 1], [1, 1.001]] with nearly aligned columns, compute det(A) as a decimal to six places.
checkpoint.hint: For a 2x2 matrix [[a,b],[c,d]], det(A) = ad - bc.
derivation: The determinant is 0.001, so this specific matrix is invertible but has nearly aligned columns.
To quantify numerical sensitivity, also compute a condition number; a small determinant by itself is scale-dependent.
checkpoint.misconception: A tiny determinant alone does not prove bad conditioning for every scaled matrix.
checkpoint.extension: Compare QR-based least squares with normal equations after perturbing the second column.

stages.practice: Derive a two-feature least-squares problem by hand; solve using QR and normal equations in Python; perturb a nearly collinear column to expose conditioning.
stages.deliverable: Hand derivation, matrix script, residual norms, condition estimates and an explicit counterexample.
acceptance: Matrix shapes and units are stated
QR and normal-equation residuals are compared on well-conditioned input
Ill-conditioning is demonstrated, not merely asserted
Interpret results with tolerance and machine precision

stages.title: 03 / Algorithms, complexity and decision tradeoffs
prerequisites: Python, discrete math, basic probability
stages.question: How do you justify an algorithm before trusting its output?

checkpoint.prompt: A directed graph has edges S->A cost 2, A->G cost 3, S->B cost 1, and B->G cost 10. What is the least path cost from S to G?
checkpoint.hint: Enumerate valid S-to-G paths and add edge costs.
derivation: S->A->G costs 2+3=5.
S->B->G costs 1+10=11.
With only these four directed edges, the optimal path cost is min(5,11)=5.
checkpoint.misconception: A locally cheap first edge does not guarantee a globally shortest path.
checkpoint.extension: Add a cycle and demonstrate why nonnegative edge costs matter for Dijkstra's algorithm.

stages.practice: Implement Dijkstra's algorithm and A* on a small weighted graph; derive a lower bound heuristic, then create an inadmissible heuristic that breaks optimality.
stages.deliverable: Reference graph, oracle results, runtime scaling measurements, and documented failure case.
acceptance: Nonnegative-edge assumption is enforced
Both methods agree with reference optimum under valid assumptions
Complexity discussion separates theory from timing
An invalid heuristic produces an explained counterexample

stages.title: 04 / Search, probabilistic inference and classical AI
prerequisites: Algorithms, probability
stages.question: When does a symbolic model make a decision that a learned model cannot explain?

checkpoint.prompt: A condition has prior probability 0.10. A test has sensitivity 0.90 and false-positive rate 0.20. What is P(condition | positive)?
checkpoint.hint: Use Bayes: true-positive mass divided by all positive-test mass.
derivation: P(condition and positive) = 0.10 x 0.90 = 0.09.
P(condition | positive) = 0.09/0.27 = 1/3, not 90%.
checkpoint.misconception: Test sensitivity is not the positive predictive value; prevalence affects the posterior.
checkpoint.extension: Recalculate at a 1% base rate and explain why the result changes.

stages.practice: Build a small Bayesian diagnostic network and search-based decision policy; show the posterior calculation, compare decisions under two priors, and identify hidden assumptions.
stages.deliverable: Explicit state graph, probability table, runnable inference and assumption audit.
acceptance: Posterior values are independently calculated
Probabilities normalize to one
Changing a prior changes or preserves the decision for an explained reason
An unsupported inference is rejected

stages.title: 05 / Statistical learning and generalization
prerequisites: Probability, linear algebra, algorithms
stages.question: Which evidence supports a claim that a model generalizes beyond its training set?

checkpoint.prompt: A classifier gets 95 of 100 training cases right and 75 of 100 untouched test cases right. What is the train-minus-test accuracy gap in percentage points?
checkpoint.hint: Convert both counts to percentages, then subtract test from train.
derivation: Training accuracy = 95/100 = 95%.
Held-out accuracy = 75/100 = 75%.
The observed difference is 95 - 75 = 20 percentage points; this alone cannot identify the cause.
checkpoint.misconception: A train/test gap can indicate overfitting or distribution shift, but is not proof of either.
checkpoint.extension: Repeat fixed-split evaluation over independent seeds and include uncertainty intervals.

stages.practice: Compare a linear baseline against a more flexible classifier on synthetic data; evaluate held-out accuracy over 20 seeds, leak a feature deliberately and quantify the inflated score.
stages.deliverable: Data-generating process, frozen splits, uncertainty intervals, model card and leakage counterexample.
acceptance: Held-out data are never used for model selection
Variance across seeds is reported
Leakage impact is quantified and labeled invalid
Claim scope stays within evaluated distribution

stages.title: 06 / Deep networks, optimization and gradient checks
prerequisites: Calculus, linear algebra, statistical learning
stages.question: Can you verify a neural network's training signal without trusting a library?

checkpoint.prompt: In a scalar gradient-descent training problem, the loss is L(w) = (w - 3)^2. Calculate the exact derivative dL/dw evaluated at w = 1.
checkpoint.hint: Differentiate the squared term using the chain rule, then substitute w = 1.
derivation: The derivative is dL/dw = 2(w - 3).
At w = 1, the derivative is 2(1 - 3) = -4.
A sufficiently small positive gradient-descent step moves w upward toward 3 because w_new = w - eta(-4).
checkpoint.misconception: A negative derivative describes the local slope and preferred descent direction; it does not mean that the nonnegative squared loss is negative.
checkpoint.extension: Check this gradient against centered finite differences for multiple step sizes.

stages.practice: Implement a two-layer network and analytic backpropagation on a tiny dataset; compare each gradient against a centered finite-difference estimate and measure sensitivity to learning rate.
stages.deliverable: Fully specified loss, gradient table, controlled training curves and a failure analysis.
acceptance: All parameters have explicit shapes
Finite-difference checks meet stated numerical tolerance
Training and validation losses remain separate
At least one unstable setting is reproduced and explained

stages.title: 07 / Attention, transformers and language modeling
prerequisites: Backpropagation, matrix multiplication, probability
stages.question: What can a causal transformer attend to, and how can you demonstrate a leak?

checkpoint.prompt: For an attention row with valid logits [0, ln(2)], what softmax weight is assigned to the second token?
checkpoint.hint: Exponentiate the logits, then normalize by their sum.
derivation: Exponentiated logits are exp(0) = 1 and exp(ln(2)) = 2.
Normalization gives the second token weight 2/(1+2) = 2/3.
This weight applies only among the allowed tokens; causal masking must exclude future positions.
checkpoint.misconception: Attention weights are normalized model coefficients, not necessarily explanations of causation.
checkpoint.extension: Mask the future token and prove an earlier output stays unchanged when a later input is altered.

stages.practice: Implement scaled dot-product attention on a three-token toy example; show row-softmax normalization, causal masking, attention weights, and a controlled mask-off counterexample.
stages.deliverable: Computed tensors, shape tests, mask invariance proof, and a documented leaking failure.
acceptance: Attention matrices have predicted shapes
Valid attention probabilities sum to one
Future-token changes cannot affect masked earlier positions
Removing the mask yields an independently reproduced leak

stages.title: 08 / Retrieval, RAG and evidence-grounded generation
prerequisites: Transformers, text processing, information retrieval basics
stages.question: When should an assistant answer, cite evidence or abstain?

checkpoint.prompt: A retrieval system returns five documents, three of which are relevant to the query. What is precision@5?
checkpoint.hint: Precision is the number of relevant retrieved results divided by the total retrieved.
derivation: There are three relevant results in five retrieved documents.
Precision@5 = 3/5 = 0.6.
Recall cannot be inferred unless the total relevant corpus documents are known.
checkpoint.misconception: Retrieval precision is not citation faithfulness; a generator may still misquote a retrieved document.
checkpoint.extension: Create unanswerable queries and measure abstention separately from retrieval success.

stages.practice: Construct a 30-document synthetic source corpus with a labeled query set; measure recall-at-k, precision of citations, unsupported answers and abstention under missing evidence.
stages.deliverable: Synthetic corpus, fixed query labels, retrieval baseline, error taxonomy, and before/after evaluation.
acceptance: Train and evaluation queries are separated
Every reported citation maps to an actual source span
Unanswerable questions trigger tested abstentions
Reported improvements include raw confusion counts

stages.title: 09 / Reinforcement learning and distributional risk
prerequisites: Probability, optimization, Markov chains
stages.question: Why can two policies with equal mean reward carry very different risks?

checkpoint.prompt: A policy returns +2 in nine episodes and -10 in one episode. What is its empirical mean return over ten episodes?
checkpoint.hint: Sum all returns including losses, and divide by the number of episodes.
derivation: Total return = 9 x 2 + 1 x (-10) = 8.
Empirical mean = 8/10 = 0.8.
The worst observed return is -10, so a positive mean hides meaningful downside risk.
checkpoint.misconception: A higher sample mean does not establish that a policy meets a tail-risk constraint.
checkpoint.extension: Compute the empirical return distribution and report lower quantiles across more trials.

stages.practice: Implement tabular Q-learning and an exact dynamic-programming reference in a small MDP; estimate a policy return distribution over 100 independent seeds and compare lower-tail outcomes.
stages.deliverable: MDP specification, Bellman checks, learning curves and return quantiles with uncertainty.
acceptance: State/action/reward/termination rules are explicit
Bellman baseline is reproduced independently
Mean and lower-tail outcomes are both reported
Seeds and evaluation protocol make the comparison repeatable

stages.title: 10 / Multi-agent AI, safety and research-grade capstone
prerequisites: All prior stages or documented equivalent evidence
stages.question: Can an AI system remain reliable when agents, tools and environments change?

checkpoint.prompt: Agent A succeeds with probability 0.80 and agent B with 0.75. Under an explicit independence assumption, what is P(both succeed)?
checkpoint.hint: If and only if the two events are independent, multiply their marginal probabilities.
derivation: Under independence P(A and B)=P(A)P(B).
If agents share a hidden environment or interact, independence may fail and this product need not hold.
checkpoint.misconception: Multi-agent success rates cannot generally be multiplied without demonstrating independence.
checkpoint.extension: Introduce a shared failure cause, measure dependence and compare joint success against 0.60.

stages.practice: Build an isolated two-agent decision benchmark with nonstationary partner behavior; compare fixed-policy and adaptive baselines, run ablation tests and introduce a tool failure with a safe fallback.
stages.deliverable: Public reproducibility package: assumptions, synthetic data, code, tests, result tables, failure cases, limitations, and primary-source citations.
acceptance: No production systems or other people's data are tested
Baselines, ablations and uncertainty are reported
At least one failed hypothesis is retained
Conclusions separate observed results from general claims
